extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Reformation history; general educated readers interested in Erasmus, Luther, and early-16th-century religious/political change
extracted.subtask_short: historical analysis of Erasmus and Luther
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-historical treatment comparing Erasmus and Luther around the time of the Reformation, focusing on personalities, methods, and the rhetorical/theological qualities that shaped reception and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperate tone and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Theses were a temperate document; Erasmus exhorts restraint: 'We ought to keep an even temper, lest it be spoiled by anger, hatred, or vainglory;' he counsels gentleness and moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid violent or vitriolic language in reformist or critical writing; gentleness, moderation, and measured reserve are presented as more effective and respectable than angry invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisive public commitment versus hedging
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus is described as 'hedging' and avoiding frank opposition, whereas Luther acts with decisive conviction—'the boldness of Luther' and willingness to 'let himself go' when compelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For leaders or agents of reform, public, clear commitment and decisiveness are necessary; hedging or excessive caution may fail to provide leadership in critical moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to common experience and multiple social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Luther's appeal succeeded because 'in Luther there spoke the monk, the priest, the scholar, the patriot, and finally the man'—his message echoed varied human experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive reform rhetoric should resonate across audiences by touching multiple relevant identities and experiences (religious, scholarly, civic, personal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not approve or condemn without reading and deliberate judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus: 'I am not so rash as to approve what I have not read, nor such a trickster as to condemn what I know nothing about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly or public evaluation requires careful reading and informed judgment rather than rumor, hearsay, or premature public condemnation/approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper forum: refute in books or by learned men, not by public shouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus criticized the practice of noisy public denunciation: he advised that things 'ought more properly to be refuted in books or discussed by learned men' rather than 'bawling out so hatefully to the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reasoned, documented counter-argument in appropriate scholarly or written forums instead of inflammatory public spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-refinement of distinctions that obscure the point
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus 'drew a picture of the thing he wanted to express and believed himself to be heightening the effect of this picture when he refined upon it until its outlines became obscured and the very effect he had aimed at was defeated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive subtlety or minute distinctions can dilute the clarity and force of an argument; keep central points clear rather than over-elaborating nuances that obscure the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reforming abusive use of practices while preserving useful institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus' stance: 'Let us amend the wrong use of these things, but let us not disturb the innocent and helpful practice itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing change, emphasize correcting abuses and preserving beneficial institutional functions rather than wholesale abolition, unless the institution cannot be reformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral teaching should emphasize individual conscience and freedom of will
rubrics_metrics.description: The Enchiridion emphasizes the function of the individual conscience in determining action: 'The freedom of the will in human action is so completely assumed that there is no need of discussing it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical instruction, per Erasmus, should appeal to individual duty and conscience rather than rely solely on external ecclesiastical authority or claims of irresistible divine action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame reform propositions as challenges to discussion and open to correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Luther's Theses 'were a challenge to discussion' and he 'put himself forward as a learner, who was prepared to change his view whenever a better one should appear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present reforms as invitations to debate and demonstration rather than as uncompromising dogma—openness to correction can strengthen legitimacy and stimulate constructive engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character and life as evidence of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus argues for considering an author's life: 'The man's way of life is approved by all... his character is so sound that not even enemies can find anything to criticise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's personal conduct and reputation influence how their ideas are received; moral probity can lend persuasive authority to scholarly or reformist claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid religious practices that appear mercantile or corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of indulgences in Germany is criticized as 'purely mercantile'—the Prince Elector accepting half the plunder to pay for a pallium made the transaction outrageously corrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices that resemble commercial exploitation undermine moral authority and provoke legitimate reformist criticism; avoid or reform procedures that give rise to perceptions of profiteering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware zeal that provokes enmity against learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus feared that too free a pen and extreme polemics would 'add to the enmity against learning' and feared the consequences of violent or intemperate discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive zeal or satirical attack risks alienating potential allies and generating backlash that harms intellectual causes; temper rhetorical strategy to protect the broader project of learning and reform.
